questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go en exchange in my 4th semester, and therefore I had to go somewhere that didn't need a transcript of records, because I had to seek a destination spot before I had gone to my first semester examens. Nevertheless, I knew that I wanted to go any other place in France than Caen, where I had already spent a séjour, and Paris, which is way too big for a countryside girl. So in reality, I didn't have many crucial aspects for my study destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I feel like the preparation before, during and also now after has taken up way too much time and energy. All the bureaucratie with little help from my host and original country. I had to change my OLA several times, I had trouble with the sites for signatures, and I feel like I had to contact a hundred different people to get the help I needed. My education highly recommends people to go abroad, so I feel like the system around should be made easier or every student with an exchange spot should get a person that can specifically help them to make the process easier. Nevertheless, I am glad I went abroad, because I have learned a lot from this very tedious process.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We had a very nice coordinator at my destination spot, but she couldn't help us very much, so the first month was horrific for me. Everything was new and I had to pretty much figure everything out by myself in my third and weakest language. I made it, but it was through blood, sweat and tears. Luckily I am quite stubborn and I persisted. The sytem in France, and especially in Perpignan, isn't as easy as in Denmark, where everything is found online. I had to go to everyone of my 11 professors and manually inscribe myself in the courses, and I didn't get a specified plan for my courses, but I had to use the overall plan for the whole university. I learned the procedure with time, but in the beginning, I felt like a fish out of water.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had an intro meeting and sightseeing of the university with my coordinator Madame Badiane, who also helped me set up af meeting with the leader of Departement des Lettres, so I could find my final courses and edit my last OLA. After this I was left to my own devices. I would have liked a bit more help in the beginning, but by persistance, I figured out all the small details on how and what to do.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think my coordinator did everything she could do, but I would have liked more help or a system that was set up make it easier for exchange students coming to the country. As an example, the university already had my course list, because they had signed my OLA, so I feel like they could have taken the time to make me a personal plan, so I could have started my classes from the first day. Instead I had to book a meeting with my department leader, and therefore I missed three days of classes, which I also got reprimanded for, but I didn't at the time know what to do but wait.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used the recommended sites from Erasmus and ended up finding a collocation in the city center on the site : Roomlala. It was very safe and I payed my fees through the website.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It gives you a natural link to the city and not just the university. I did my fitness, drank my coffees etc. in the city with the locals. And I also had a French person who could help me and guide me a bit, which was nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't really see the CROUS, where the other students lived, but I heard a lot of them complain of the facilities. But again I only know the appartement that I lived in, which was a private owner.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very though. I changed my OLA several times before arriving. Afterwards I had to sign myself up manually in every course - this took a lot of time, and in some of my courses I didn't have acces to the platform MOODLE before the exams, because the professor couldn't or forgot to add me. Some of my classes I had to ask every week the whole semester to be added, because of complications. I did figure it out, but it was way more difficult than I had imagined and than I believe it had to be.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had a meeting with the leader of my department, who changed the courses from my OLA that she didn't think would benefit me. I had to make my own plan from the overall university plan of courses. Afterwards I introduced myself to every professor and asked them to add me to the course list as well as the Moodle platform. Some of them had to be asked several times.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had my coordinator, Madame Badiane, who tried to help me, but other than that, I felt very much alone. Maybe there was other alternatives, but I didn't really know what to do except try to understand the procedures myself. It took time, but eventually I got it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had eleven classes that I pretty much chose myself with a bit of guidance. But I didn't get rejected from any of the classes that I wanted, even those they thought would be too difficult. My departement leader simply said I would have to try for a couple of weeks and then decide if I could do it. I didn't end up changing any of my courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You will figure it out. It is a new system, and it will be tough at first, but when you return home, you will find yourself stronger, smarter and more efficient.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very hard, but very interesting and I learned a lot.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had courses on all three years of License de Lettres even though I was on my second year in my danish program. It went well even though it sometimes was tough and hard work. I chose my courses from intresse and from which courses they should be equal to in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In Denmark we have fewer courses with larger materiale, but in Perpignan, we had a lot of smaller courses with more in-depth thinking. In Perpignan I spend more than 25 hours at the university in classe every week and also had a lot of homework, reading etc. to do - so a much larger work load, but even though I was very stressed, I also feel like I have accomplished a great deal in a short time. I like the danish structure more, but the themes and course materiales in Perpignan was very interesting.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1) Littérature Classique - L2
2) Littérature 19e-20e - L2
3) Littérature Comparée 
4) Introduction Histoire Art Contemporain - L3 
5) Littérature et Philosophie - L3 
6) De Grèce à nous - L3 
7) Tuto Erasmus Mardi - Erasmus 
8) Tuto Erasmus Jeudi - Erasmus
9) Techniques Expression Ecrite - L1 
10) Latin - L1 
11) Intercompréhension - L3

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I liked Littérature comparée, Introduction Histoire Art Contemporain and Techniques Expression Ecrite the most. Littérature comparée compared two books in one genre, which was very cool. Histoire Art Contemporain was a course of show and tell, where we looked at paintings from different significant painters that created modernity. Techniques Expression Ecrite was a course, where we learned to write a shortstory in a specific universe of an author, in my case Lovecraft.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't really meet unexpected costs, but I also had enough money to not worry over budgets and such. I did what I wanted and bought what I needed - of course with reason.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was more expensive than I thought

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Lots of free sports, concerts, movies and clubs at the university. The only problem was I didn't have time to try it all.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Danse, music, ceramics, concerts, trips etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Visit the smaller cities around your host town - if in Perpignan go to : Céret, Cannet-en-Rousillon, Thuir, Castelnou. And if you have time go to : Carcassonne and Cadaqués (the house of Salvador Dali is situated here).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Just do what you enjoy. Some people want to see and do a lot - I personally preferred creating a life in Perpignan, just as the one I have in Denmark, with friends, sports, shopping and relaxing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had been to France several times beforehand, so I knew a lot already. It was quite easy for me, but nevertheless, I missed the culture I knew from home. One can adjust, but you never really become them.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really. I only befriended the other exchange students. For us Erasmus the semester is special, but one have to remember that it is just another university year for the people who always lives at your destination. They are not rude for not wanting to become your friend, they are simply living their lives. I understand it, and it was fine for me with the other Erasmus, who understood my position. The French students were friendly and also helped you if you asked, but they kept to their own friend groupes.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The French are a bit more relaxed about time, which meant I waited a lot. And they also speak a lot to strangers, which meant I had a lot of weird conversations in the streets.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Sitting at a café for hours just existing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Trust yourself, you'll figure it out, even though the sytem is hard to understand.
2) Find strength in the other exchange students.
3) Do what gives your time meaning : I used more time on university than exploring, but a lot of my Erasmus friends did the opposite, and we both had meaningful stays, so do what makes sense for you.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The city of Perpignan has a lot of people of lower means, so take caution and think about where and when you are walking alone. It isn't dangerous everywhere, but one must be careful.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The growth in my person and in my abilities in French.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Living, exciting and doing the bureaucratie in a language that you don't fully master.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
